lesson.title: Text as Data: The str Type
lesson.summary: The str type stores ordered, immutable sequences of characters, accessed by index or slice, and it never mixes automatically with numbers the way some other languages allow.
lesson.body:
A string, written as str in Python, is a sequence of characters used to represent text: a name, a sentence, a single letter, or even an empty piece of text with nothing in it at all. You create a string literal by wrapping characters in either single quotes ('hello') or double quotes ("hello"), and Python treats both forms identically, which is convenient when the text itself needs to contain one kind of quote, like "it's raining" or 'she said "go"'.

Strings are one of Python's sequence types, meaning the characters inside have a defined order and can be accessed by position, or index, starting at 0. Given word = "python", word[0] is "p" and word[5] is "n", the last character, since indexing starts counting from zero rather than one. Strings also support slicing to pull out a range of characters: word[0:3] produces "pyt", taking everything from index 0 up to, but not including, index 3.

A property that trips up many beginners is that strings in Python are immutable: once a string object is created, none of its individual characters can be changed in place. Trying word[0] = "P" raises a TypeError, because assignment into a string is not allowed. To get a modified version of a string, you build a new one, often using string methods that return a fresh string rather than editing the original. Consider this trace:

greeting = "hello"
loud = greeting.upper()
print(greeting)
print(loud)

Calling greeting.upper() does not touch greeting at all; it returns a brand new string "HELLO" and hands it to loud. The first print still shows "hello", unchanged, and only the second print shows "HELLO". This same pattern, a method that reads from an object and returns a new value rather than modifying the original, applies to most string methods, including .lower(), .strip(), and .replace().

Strings connect closely to the numeric types covered earlier in this unit. The text "42" and the integer 42 look related but are not interchangeable: "42" + 1 raises a TypeError for the same reason name + 1 failed in the data types lesson, because Python will not silently decide whether + means numeric addition or text concatenation when the types disagree. Converting deliberately between text and numbers, using functions like int() and str(), is exactly what the type conversion lessons later in this unit are built around.

Because a string is a sequence, it also works directly with a for loop, stepping through one character at a time: for letter in "cat": print(letter) prints "c", then "a", then "t", each on its own line, in order. Strings additionally support special escape sequences inside their quotes, such as \n for a newline and \t for a tab, and triple quotes, written as either """ or ''', for text that needs to span multiple lines without adding explicit \n characters throughout. These features are what make str flexible enough to represent everything from a single character to an entire paragraph, while still behaving as one consistent, ordered, immutable type.
